newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran ready to refine Kazakh oil under swap deal.
newsitem.headline: Iran ready to refine Kazakh oil under swap deal.

text.p: Iran's Tehran and Tabriz oil refineries will receive and refine the first trial delivery of Kazakh crude next week under a bilateral swap deal, an Iranian energy official said on Sunday.

"The crude comes by pipeline next week. We are going to refine Kazakh crude temporarily to get some information. It will be a trial run," said Sayyed Reza Kasaeizadeh, director of refining affairs at the state-run National Iranian Refining and Distribution Company (NIORDC).

The United States, which has imposed wide-ranging sanctions against Tehran's oil sector, has viewed the swap deal with concern because some major U.S. firms are investing in oil projects in the Central Asian state.
Almaty has said that only state-owned oil, and not output from Western firms in Kazakhstan, would be swapped with Iran.
Under the deal Iran will initially refine 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Kazakh crude blended with its own Iran Light crude at Tehran and Tabriz.
After two years the amount supplied to the two northern Iranian refineries will increase to 120,000 bpd.
"We are planning to increase this amount to 120,000 bpd in five years' time. We are intending to do the same with Turkmenistan," Kasaeizadeh said.
In return, Kazakhstan will be entitled to the same value of crude oil at Iranian export terminals in the Gulf or at Iran's storage facilities in Europe such as at Rotterdam.
Kasaeizadeh said that the expected Kazakh crude that would be sent to Tehran and Tabriz refineries would have a higher salt and nickel content than Iranian crude.
"It is very difficult to run Kazakh crude. The refineries were designed to run off Iran Light," he said.
Tehran, resisting a campaign by Washington to isolate it politically and economically, has tried to increase its ties with its Central Asian neighbours and other states.

Trial shipments of Kazakh crude across the Caspian Sea to an Iranian port began earlier this month and Iranian officials are keen to ensure that Almaty can guarantee the steady delivery of crude for Tehran and Tabriz.
So far, Almaty has had to rely on neighbouring Russia's pipeline system to export its growing oil output.
The deal allows Iran to save on the cost of pumping crude produced at its prolific southern fields to refineries in the far north of the country.
No date has yet been set for the first 100,000 tonne-plus shipment of Iranian crude from the Gulf that will be lifted by Almaty.
